beats.t: Evolution is history, and history normally happens only once.
Stephen Jay Gould asked what would happen if we could rewind the tape of life and play it again.
With a flask of yeast, we can. This film walks through how the experiment is done, and why each step exists.

scenes.title: Why evolve life in a flask

beats.t: In nature we see only the survivors: never the losers, never the alternatives.
Control. We choose the ancestor and the environment, so we know what changed.
Replication. Many populations start identical, so we can tell what is repeatable from what is chance.
Time travel. Yeast survive freezing, so ancestors can be revived and raced against their descendants.
Scale. One 100 mL flask holds about 10¹⁰ cells, and about eight generations pass every 48 hours.
Most microbial evolution experiments follow one recipe. Each step removes one source of ambiguity.
Six steps make the classic experiment. Barcoding adds two more: tag every cell, then count the tags.
Streak the ancestor across agar so the cells thin out, then pick one isolated colony: the descendants of a single cell.
Now every cell carries the same genome. Any genetic difference that appears later must be a new mutation.
Skip this, and a variant that rises might have been there from the start. New and old would look the same.
The ancestor's genome is sequenced once. Every evolved genome is compared against it.
The yeast grow in M3, a defined minimal medium. Glucose runs out first; every other nutrient is in excess.
Defined means every ingredient is known and weighed, so the selective pressure is the same in every flask, every week.
M3 also lacks uracil. Only cells that keep the barcode construct, which carries the URA3 gene, can grow in it.
100 mL of medium in a 500 mL flask, 30 °C, shaken at about 200 rpm. Each of these is part of the environment.
Over 48 hours the cells wake up, ferment glucose, switch to respiring ethanol, and stop.
Then 400 µL of the 100 mL culture moves into fresh medium: a 1 in 250 dilution.
250 ≈ 2⁸. To refill the flask the cells must double about eight times, so each cycle is about eight generations.
The environment is a cycle of feast and famine. Selection acts on every phase: waking fast, growing fast, switching well.
Each transfer is a random draw of about 4 × 10⁷ cells. A mutant that is still rare can be left behind by luck.
A new mutant with a 5% advantage must reach roughly 1/s = 20 cells before chance stops mattering. Most never get there.
A large bottleneck also supplies mutations: N × μ ≈ 4 × 10⁷ × 10⁻⁶, about 40 new mutants worth more than 5% every generation.
After every transfer, the leftover culture is spun down, resuspended in 30% glycerol, split into three cryovials and stored at −80 °C.
The frozen record can be revived: ancestors raced against descendants, or evolution replayed from any point.
Populations are run in replicate. When independent populations hit the same gene again and again, chance is an unlikely explanation.
Fitness is relative. The evolved strain is mixed with a marked ancestor, and their ratio is followed over several cycles.
Why not just measure growth rate? A strain can grow faster and still lose the flask because it wakes up later.
Frequencies change as df/dt = f (s − s̄). For two strains, the log of their ratio is a straight line whose slope is s.
Sequencing a whole population detects a mutation only once it reaches about 1% of the cells.
By then the race is decided. Thousands of mutations arose and were lost or outcompeted below that line.
The classic experiment shows the winners, but not the race.
Levy et al. (2015) followed lineages instead of mutations. Before evolution starts, each cell receives a DNA barcode.
A barcode is a random stretch of about 20 bases between fixed sequences, inside an artificial intron of the URA3 gene.
Random: 4²⁰ ≈ 10¹² possible tags for a few hundred thousand cells. Neutral: spliced out, never expressed. Inherited by every descendant.
When a lineage gains a beneficial mutation, its barcode count rises. The mutation is detected by its effect, before anyone knows what it is.
Strain SHA185 carries a landing pad on chromosome II: Cre recombinase behind a galactose promoter, half of URA3, and a lox site.
A plasmid library (pBar3) carries the barcodes beside the other half of URA3. On galactose, Cre stitches a plasmid into the pad.
Only a correct insertion rebuilds URA3, so only barcoded cells grow without uracil. The leftover lox66/71 site makes the insertion one-way.
In practice, each transformation yields a limited number of barcodes. Schmidlin et al. (2024) ran 24 transformations and kept 14: about 300,000 barcodes.
They discarded transformations with 'monster' barcodes above 1% of cells: with too many cells, one barcode can collect several different mutations.
The barcoded pool is evolved exactly as before: M3, 48-hour cycles, about 4 × 10⁷ cells per transfer. Levy et al. ran two replicates for 168 generations.
Barcoding is slightly mutagenic, so many beneficial mutations already exist at the start. The number of rising lineages peaks after a few dozen generations.
Every transfer is frozen. Later, the barcodes in each sample are extracted, amplified and counted.

scenes.title: Counting barcodes I · Extract the DNA

beats.t: Zymolyase digests the yeast cell wall; a detergent then opens the cells and releases their DNA.
Guanidine thiocyanate, a chaotropic salt, makes DNA stick to a silica membrane at about pH 5. Washes remove proteins and salts.
A low-salt buffer releases clean DNA. About 200 ng is the DNA of 10⁷ cells, so every barcode is represented by many template copies.
Step one runs only 3 cycles. Primers bind the fixed sequences around the barcode and add a random 8-base UMI on each side, plus a sample index.
Each original molecule gets its own pair of UMIs. Copies made later share them, so duplicates can be recognised and counted once.
Magnetic SPRI beads clean up the product. The bead-to-sample ratio sets a size cutoff: amplicons bind to the beads; short primers wash away.
Step two runs about 25–35 cycles with primers that add the Illumina adapters and indexes. A 0.8× bead cleanup removes primer dimers.

scenes.title: Counting barcodes III · Reads to frequencies

beats.t: Libraries are quantified, pooled in equal amounts and sequenced. Dual indexes keep reads from being assigned to the wrong sample.
Each read is parsed into UMI, index, priming site and barcode. Barcodes are matched to the known list, allowing up to two errors.
Identical UMI–barcode pairs are PCR duplicates and collapse to one count. A barcode's count divided by all counts is its frequency.
Rules of thumb: pass at least 100 cells per barcode (better 1,000), read at least 100 reads per barcode per time point, stay under 50 generations.
The model: each lineage changes as dfᵢ/dt = fᵢ (sᵢ − s̄), where s̄ = Σ fᵢ sᵢ is the mean fitness of the flask.
Then ln(fᵢ / f_ref) is a straight line in time. Its slope is sᵢ, measured against a reference set to zero.
With five time points, s comes from a weighted fit or a maximum-likelihood fit to the read counts. Points with few reads count less.
Neutral barcoded lineages show the noise floor: drift at every bottleneck plus the sampling of reads.
In Levy's replicate E1, about 25,000 of roughly 500,000 lineages carried beneficial mutations.
Mutations worth more than 5% arose at about 10⁻⁶ per cell per generation. Most benefits were 2–5%.
Whole-population sequencing would have seen about 15 of them.

scenes.title: Measuring hundreds of mutants at once

beats.t: Adaptive clones keep their barcodes, so hundreds can be pooled and measured in one flask.
The pool is mixed with about 90% ancestor (95% in strong drug). Each mutant then races the ancestor, and the mean fitness barely moves.
The ancestor must not use up the reads. Kinsler et al. (2020) cut its barcode with the enzyme ApaLI; Schmidlin et al. used an ancestor with no barcode.
About 1% barcoded ancestral control strains define fitness = 0 and anchor every slope.
Schmidlin et al. (2024) asked whether drug-resistant mutants all pay the same costs elsewhere.
Twelve evolutions from one pool: fluconazole (FLU) at three doses, radicicol (RAD) at three doses, four combinations, DMSO, and no drug.
Doses came from plate-reader growth curves: 'low' did not slow growth, 'high' cut growth rate by about 15%, so barcode diversity survived.
After 3–6 cycles, while many lineages were rising, 2,000 colonies per condition (1,000 in high FLU) were scraped and pooled: about 21,000 isolates.
That pool was competed in all 12 conditions, twice each: 24 competitions of about 40 generations.
774 lineages had more than 500 reads in all 12 conditions: 9,288 fitness values.
Each lineage's 12 fitnesses form a fingerprint. Standardised and embedded with UMAP, they fall into 6 clusters plus the controls.
Clusters differ in tradeoffs. PDR1/PDR3 mutants resist high fluconazole; SUR1/UPC2 mutants win only at low doses; some RAD-resistant mutants also win with no drug.
Kinsler et al. (2020) used the same idea with 292 mutants in 45 environments: near home a few traits explain fitness; far away, hidden ones matter.

scenes.title: Whole-genome sequencing I · Colony to library

beats.t: A barcode says which lineage is fit, not why. To find the mutation, single clones are isolated and their whole genomes sequenced.
Cells from the pooled sample are plated, single colonies are grown in YPD, and their genomic DNA is purified.
Tagmentation: bead-bound transposomes cut the genome into fragments and attach adapter sequences in a single step (Illumina DNA Prep).
A short PCR of 6–10 cycles adds unique dual indexes. A double-sided bead selection keeps fragments of the right size.

scenes.title: Whole-genome sequencing II · Sequencing by synthesis

beats.t: On the flow cell, each fragment is copied in place into a cluster of about a thousand identical molecules.
Each cycle adds one fluorescent, reversibly blocked base to every cluster. A camera records the colour, the block and dye are removed, and the next cycle begins.
150 cycles from each end give 2 × 150 base paired reads: millions of them per genome.

scenes.title: Whole-genome sequencing III · Finding the mutation

beats.t: Reads are aligned to the reference genome (sacCer3). They pile up, so every base is read many times over.
Where the reads disagree with the reference, GATK calls a variant. In a haploid clone, a real mutation appears in almost every read.
Variants also present in the ancestor, or shared by many unrelated lineages, are background and are removed. SnpEff names the gene and the amino-acid change.
Typically one or a few mutations per lineage: PDR1, PDR3, SUR1, UPC2, HDA1, IRA1… Changes in ploidy are checked separately by DNA staining and flow cytometry.
Every step exists to remove one ambiguity.
Twenty random letters of DNA, copied faithfully, let us count evolution as it happens.
